solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Be proud and resolute going outside (5,3)

indicators.note: STOUT goes round the outside of AND

blocks.note: stout = resolute, as in a stout defence
the word itself, taken as printed

explanation.surface: Advice to stand tall and firm when you step out into the world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Proud' here is the physical sense, sticking out from a surface, as a nail stands proud of the wood; 'and', which looks like a joining word, is the letters placed inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that is proud projects beyond its surroundings, which is exactly what it does when it stands out.

clue.text: Perhaps May article on Salvation Army (7)

indicators.note: perhaps marks the definition as one example of a wider class, here a first name that one famous May carried

blocks.note: the usual initials for the Salvation Army

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether May will see an article written about the Salvation Army.
explanation.walkthrough: May looks like the month, or a verb of permission; it is the surname of Theresa May, the former British prime minister.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: May is the surname of one famous bearer of the first name, the former British prime minister (2016-2019).

clue.text: Girl raised grouse on island (5)

indicators.note: in a down clue, raising a word writes it bottom to top

blocks.note: to grouse is to moan, complain

explanation.surface: A girl kicks up a fuss about something while stuck on an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grouse' looks like the game bird, which fits an island scene, but it is the verb meaning complain.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the answer is a girl's first name, Hebrew in origin and borne by Ruth's mother-in-law in the Bible.

clue.text: No spring chicken daring to go topless (3)

indicators.note: in a down clue the top of the word is its first letter, which is removed

blocks.note: BOLD without its first letter B

explanation.surface: An older woman shows some daring by going topless.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a daring older sunbather, and the definition is the idiom for someone past their youth.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who is no spring chicken is no longer young, that is old.

clue.text: Check striker fit for international? (4,5)

blocks.note: a match is struck to light it, so it is a striker

explanation.surface: A manager checks whether the centre forward is fit enough to play for his country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Striker' pretends to be a footballer; it is a match. A test match is an international cricket or rugby game.
explanation.definitionFit: A Test match is a game between two national sides, so it is an international.

clue.text: Play involving black fellow (4)

indicators.note: TOY involves, that is takes in, B

blocks.note: to play with something is to toy with it

explanation.surface: A drama whose plot centres on a black man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Play' looks like a noun, a drama, but it is the verb toy. Crossword fellows are often any man's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Toby is a man's name, and a fellow is a man.

clue.text: Fish sandwiches to present without thought (4,3)

indicators.note: TROUT holds TO between its slices

blocks.note: the word itself, taken as printed

explanation.surface: A fish sandwich handed over without a second's thought.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sandwiches' fits the lunch picture but is a verb here, meaning puts between.
explanation.definitionFit: To trot out an excuse is to offer a stock one without thinking.

clue.text: Intolerant sort to leave in short while (5)

indicators.note: 'in' places the word before it inside the one after, so the leaving sits in the short while

blocks.note: wait a bit = wait a short while

explanation.surface: Someone narrow-minded is told to clear off for a little while.
explanation.walkthrough: A bit of time is a short while, as in back in a bit.
explanation.definitionFit: A bigot is a person intolerant of other views or groups.

clue.text: Leading character is somewhat lecherous (4)

indicators.note: only some of the next word is used

blocks.note: the letters sit inside this word, after its first three and before its last two

explanation.surface: The star of the story turns out to be a bit of a lech.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a verdict on a character; lec(HERO)us holds the answer inside the one long word.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the protagonist, the leading character, of a story, film or play.

clue.text: Drive away duck circling one small lake (8)

indicators.note: DODGE goes round the other letters

blocks.note: to duck a blow is to dodge it
S = small, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: Chasing off a duck that keeps paddling round a pond.
explanation.walkthrough: The duck looks like the bird to be driven off; it is the verb meaning dodge, split D…ODGE round I, S and L.
explanation.definitionFit: To dislodge something is to force it out of place, driving it away.

clue.text: Welsh aim wrecked in London borough (8)

indicators.note: the letters are wrecked and rebuilt

explanation.surface: A Welshman's plans come to grief on a trip to London.
explanation.walkthrough: Lewisham is a borough of south-east London; the clue sets Wales against London to hide it.
explanation.definitionFit: Lewisham is one of the thirty-two London boroughs.

clue.text: Six-footer encountered in verse? (9)

blocks.note: the surface reads a very tall person; in prosody a foot is a unit of rhythm, so this is something six feet long
the question mark admits the pun: this six-footer is met in poetry, not on a basketball court

explanation.surface: A very tall person turns up in a poem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Six-footer' suggests a tall person; in poetry a foot is a unit of rhythm, and a line of six feet is a hexameter.
explanation.definitionFit: A hexameter is a line of verse made up of six metrical feet.

clue.text: Too much love for German fellow (4)

blocks.note: OTT = over the top, too much

explanation.surface: A German man is said to be excessively in love.
explanation.walkthrough: OTT is British slang for over the top, overdone.
explanation.definitionFit: Otto is a typical German man's name.

clue.text: Organ swell that might hamper listener? (6)

definitions.note: the definition is a descriptive phrase, standing for a thing that might hamper a listener

blocks.note: the ear is an organ of the body

explanation.surface: A church organ's swell pedal gets in the way of someone trying to listen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Organ swell' reads as the musical instrument's volume control; the organ is the ear and swell is wax, as a growing moon waxes.
explanation.definitionFit: A build-up of earwax blocks the ear and dulls a listener's hearing.

clue.text: Material from most evil news boss (7)

blocks.note: the worst is the most evil
ED = editor, the boss of a newspaper

explanation.surface: A scoop sourced from a thoroughly wicked newspaper editor.
explanation.walkthrough: Worsted is a smooth woollen cloth, used for suits.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the answer is a smooth woollen cloth named after Worstead in Norfolk, one kind of material.

clue.text: Shows disapproval about our heartless lecturers (6)

indicators.note: TUTS goes about the other letters
OUR loses its middle letter U

blocks.note: to tut is to click the tongue in disapproval

explanation.surface: Students click their tongues at their spineless teachers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Our' looks like a possessive attaching to the lecturers; it is fodder that loses its heart.
explanation.definitionFit: University tutors teach and lecture students.

clue.text: Go berserk in high-scoring Lord’s game? (3,4)

blocks.note: to go wild, lose all restraint; an idiom with a verb, in 3,4
Lord's is the London cricket ground; in a high-scoring match the runs come riotously

explanation.surface: A cricketer loses his temper during a big-hitting match at Lord's.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord's is the London cricket ground; the question mark flags the playful reading of RUN RIOT, where runs are what go wild.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom twice over: to go wild without restraint, and, read literally, a game in which runs pile up riotously.

clue.text: Addict from southeast in ancient city (4)

indicators.note: 'in' places the compass point inside the city, as if the south-east quarter lay within its walls

blocks.note: Ur, the Sumerian city, is crosswords' favourite ancient city

explanation.surface: An addict hails from the south-east corner of an old city.
explanation.walkthrough: A user is a drug user, hence an addict.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the drugs sense: someone who takes drugs habitually is described by the shorter word.

clue.text: Sell battered fish over time (5)

indicators.note: FISH is battered out of shape
in a down clue, the fish sits over the T

explanation.surface: A chip shop takes a long time to sell its battered fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Battered' fits the chip-shop picture but means knocked about, rearranged. To shift stock is trade slang for selling it.
explanation.definitionFit: Shops that shift goods sell them, moving them off the shelves.

clue.text: Wood in stacks sheltering a pig (8)

indicators.note: MANY shelters A HOG inside it

explanation.surface: A pig takes cover among piles of logs in the woods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stacks' looks like woodpiles, fitting the scene; it means lots, many.
explanation.definitionFit: Mahogany is a hard reddish-brown wood.

clue.text: Italian city an ego destroyed (5)

indicators.note: the letters are knocked apart and rebuilt

explanation.surface: A visit to an Italian city crushes someone's self-importance.
explanation.walkthrough: The Italian city is Genoa, the northern port.
explanation.definitionFit: Genoa is a port city in north-west Italy.

clue.text: Tyrant adroit manoeuvring around court (8)

indicators.note: the letters of ADROIT are manoeuvred into a new order
the rearranged letters go around CT

explanation.surface: A despot skilfully plots his moves around the royal court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Manoeuvring' reads as political scheming, fitting a tyrant at court; it is the instruction to rearrange ADROIT.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an absolute ruler who holds unchecked power, as tyrants do.

clue.text: Strange Caribbean spirit (3)

blocks.note: old-fashioned British slang for odd or peculiar, as in 'a ___ do'
the spirit is the drink, distilled from sugar cane across the Caribbean

explanation.surface: A ghostly presence haunts a Caribbean island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirit' suggests a ghost, which fits 'Strange'; it is the drink. RUM meaning odd is old-fashioned British slang, as in a rum do.
explanation.definitionFit: Rum is both an odd thing and a spirit made from sugar cane in the Caribbean.

clue.text: Turned on by Irish film genre (4)

indicators.note: something turned faces the other way, so the word after it is written back to front

explanation.surface: Someone finds an Irish crime movie thrilling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned on' reads as a phrase meaning excited; split it and 'Turned' works on 'on' alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Noir, short for film noir, is a genre of dark crime films.

clue.text: Boss in educational activity mostly (4)

indicators.note: most of the word is kept, dropping its last letter

blocks.note: STUDY without its last letter Y

explanation.surface: The head teacher sits in on a lesson for most of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boss' looks like a manager; it is a raised knob or stud, as on a shield.
explanation.definitionFit: A boss is a round raised ornament, the same thing as a stud.

clue.text: Force breaches defences (8)

blocks.note: to ram is to force, drive through

explanation.surface: An army smashes through a castle's defences.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads as one battle report, so 'breaches' looks like the verb of the sentence; it is a second piece of wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Ramparts are defensive walls, the defences of a fort.
